Hatchlings of the Rough-legged buzzard emerge at a mass of approximately 60 grams [Ww0 = approximately 60 grams], a value that reflects the considerable yolk reserves typical of a large Arctic raptor. Nestlings are brooded intensively for the first weeks of life, during which they progress through rapid feather development before achieving first flight. The time since birth at fledging is 41 days [tx = 41 days] under the thermal conditions of an active nest environment maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a duration that aligns closely with fledging periods documented in other high-latitude Buteo species. This relatively brief nestling phase is ecologically adaptive, permitting the young to vacate the exposed tundra nest site before the peak of the brief Arctic summer wanes. The mass of newly hatched young is modest relative to the ultimate size of the adults, setting the stage for a period of exceptionally rapid somatic growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning of small mammals.

Under an incubation temperature regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the eggs of the Rough-legged buzzard hatch after an average period of approximately 29.25 days [ab = approximately 29.25 days], with reported ranges spanning 28 to 32 days. This developmental duration is unremarkable among medium-sized raptors but is noteworthy for its slight sensitivity to thermal variation in the exposed nest scrapes typical of this species. The wet weight at birth is recorded as 42.31 grams [Wwb = 42.31 grams], a figure that represents the mass of the hatchling after internal absorption of the remaining yolk sac. This initial body size imposes strong selective pressure on the parents to begin provisioning almost immediately, as the chicks transition quickly from ectothermic dependence to the endothermic demands of growth. The moderate hatchling mass reflects an interesting trade-off between producing a sufficiently developed chick and the constraints of egg size imposed by the female's pelvic dimensions and migratory energy budget.

Considerable sexual size dimorphism is apparent in this species. The ultimate wet weight for female Rough-legged buzzards reaches 1027 grams [Wwi = 1027 grams], making them substantially larger than males, whose ultimate wet weight for males is recorded at 824.6 grams [Wwi = 824.6 grams]. This degree of reversed sexual dimorphism, where females outweigh males by roughly twenty percent, is characteristic of many diurnal raptors and is often linked to the female's role in egg production and extended incubation. The larger body size in females allows for the accumulation of substantial endogenous nutrient stores necessary for clutch formation during the early Arctic spring when prey availability is still low. Males, being lighter and more agile, may be more efficient at hunting across the vast territories required to provision the female and the nestlings. This size disparity becomes evident early in the juvenile period and stabilizes as the birds approach their first winter.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this Arctic predator is governed by both physiological readiness and the demanding environmental conditions of its breeding range. Under an ambient regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], puberty is attained at 123 days since birth [tp = 123 days since birth], a stage that coincides with the completion of the juvenile molt and the acquisition of adult plumage. However, behavioral and ecological factors typically delay actual first breeding beyond this physiological milestone. Field studies indicate that under the same thermal conditions, the time since birth at first brood is 2 years since birth [tR = 2 years since birth], reflecting the time required for young birds to establish territories and develop the foraging proficiency necessary to support a clutch at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This two-year delay is a common life-history pattern among large raptors, where a steep learning curve for hunting success postpones the age of first successful reproduction. The attainment of full adult mass, particularly in females, is also a prerequisite for successful nesting.

The annual reproductive output of the Rough-legged buzzard is constrained by the short Arctic breeding season and the cyclic abundance of its primary prey, lemmings. Under optimal conditions maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], females typically produce 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], with an average of 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch]. This combination yields a maximum reproduction rate of 4 eggs per year [Ri = 4 eggs per year]. These values represent the maximum observed in a single season, as clutch size is facultatively adjusted downward during years of prey scarcity. The overall maximum longevity for wild individuals is estimated at 18.8 years [am = 18.8 years] at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a considerable lifespan that allows for multiple reproductive attempts across the bird's lifetime. This extended lifespan is typical of a slower life-history strategy, buffering the population against the extreme interannual variation in breeding success that characterizes high-latitude ecosystems. The capacity for long-term survival is also reflected in their robust physiological resilience.
